body: SALAH-UD-DIN, J.- Through this single judgment, we intend to decide the instant Criminal Appeal No. 396-M of 2024, titled “Muhammad Salar v. State & another,” along with the connected Criminal Appeal No. 395-M of 2024, titled “Muhammad Salar v. State,” Criminal Appeal No. 18-M of 2025, titled “Haroon-ur-Rashid v. State & others,” and Criminal Revision No. 06-M of 2025, titled “Haroon-ur- Rashid v. State & others.” All these matters are byproduct of one and the same judgment dated 21.12.2024, rendered by the learned Additional Sessions Judge/Samarbagh, Camp Court at Lal Qila, District Dir Lower, in Sessions Case No. 30 of 2021, arising out of FIR No. 165 dated 12.08.2021, registered U/Ss 302 and 34, P.P.C., at Police Station Lal Qila, District Dir Lower. Upon conclusion of the trial, the learned trial Court convicted and sentenced the appellant, as follows:- Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din “27. In the light of above evaluation of evidence extending benefit of doubt to accused Said Ayub, he is hereby acquitted of charges leveled against him. While accused Muhammad Salar son of Said Ayub aged about 32 years resident of Khyber Muhallah Kumbar Tehsil Lal Qilla District Dir Lower, having been found guilty of committing Qatl-e-Amd of deceased Said Haroon is hereby convicted under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code. Since there was no pre-concert rather the occurrence took place at the spur of moment, and accused Muhammad Salar on arrival to the spot witnessing altercation of complainant party with his father accused Said Ayub in a heat of passion resorted to firing on deceased, complainant therefore considering such aspect of the case as mitigating circumstance, accused Muhammad Salar is sentenced to imprisonment for life as Ta'zir. The convict shall also pay Rs. 2,00,0000/- (two million) as compensation U/S 544- A of the Criminal Procedure Code to the legal heirs of deceased and in default he shall undergo six-months simple imprisonment. Benefit of section 382-B Cr PC is extended in favour of convict.”

2. Likewise, in a separate Sessions Case No. 16/AA of 2021, arising out of FIR No. 208 dated 15.09.2021, registered U/S 15 of the Arms Act at Police Station Lal Qila, District Dir Lower, the appellant, upon conclusion of the trial, was convicted and sentenced by the learned trial Court as follows:- “12. In view of the above discussion, I have reached to an irresistible conclusion that the accused has been guilty of an offence punishable u/s 15 of Arms Act for possessing pistol 30 bore with two magazines and 11 live rounds of the same bore, for which he' could not produce any valid license or permit. The seized weapon was used in the crime reported vide case FIR No. 165 dated 12/08/2021 under section 302-34 PPC of P.S Lal Qilla. The prosecution has successfully proved charge against accused facing trial through reliable, trust worthy and confidence inspiring evidence, free from all reasonable doubts. Accused facing trial Muhammad Salar son of Said Ayub is therefore, convicted under section 15 of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Arms Act and is sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for three years. He is further sentenced to pay fine in the sum of Rs. 5000/- or in default of payment of fine to suffer simple imprisonment for one-month. Benefit of Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din section 382-B of the Cr PC is extended to the accused facing trial. The sentence awarded to the convict shall run concurrently with sentence of life imprisonment awarded to the convict in the connected main FIR No. 165 dated 12/08/2021 under section 302-34 PPC registered at P.S Lal Qilla. Convict Muhammad Salar is in custody he is therefore, sent to the District Jail Timergara, through conviction warrant. Case property stands confiscated to the State.”
underline supplied 3. Arguments of learned counsel for parties, as well as learned Addl: A.G for State were heard and requestioned record gone through with their valuable assistance.

4. As per the prosecution case, the injured, now deceased, namely Said Haroon, reported the occurrence to the local police while he was admitted to the Emergency Ward of Lal Qila Hospital. He stated that, on the fateful night, after offering Maghrib prayer, he, along with his brother, namely Said Ayub, and his sons, was present at his house. In the meanwhile, an altercation ensued between his sons and brother over the partition of property. When the complainant intervened to pacify the rival parties, his brother, Said Ayub, and nephew, Muhammad Salar (the appellant herein), took-out their respective pistols and opened fire upon the complainant-party. As a result of the firing allegedly made by the appellant, the complainant sustained Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din firearm injuries to the left side of his chest/arm and a finger of his right hand, whereas he escaped unhurt from the firing attributed to his co-accused, Said Ayub. Besides the complainant, the occurrence was allegedly witnessed by his son, Said Haroon, son-inlaw, Umar Farooq, and other inmates of the house. The motive behind the occurrence was stated to be a dispute over landed property. On the basis of the complainant’s report, a Murasila (Ex. PW-1/2) was prepared, which subsequently culminated in the registration of the instant FIR at the police station concerned against the appellant and his co-accused. Initially, the case was registered U/S 324, P.P.C. However, following the subsequent death of the injured, section 302, P.P.C., was added to the already registered FIR.

5. It is an admitted position that the present appellant, namely Muhammad Salar, is the sole accused whose role in the murder of Said Haroon, the injured who subsequently succumbed to his injuries, is under consideration. The prosecution has attributed a specific motive to the occurrence, i.e. a dispute over landed property. The record Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din further reveals that the occurrence took place at the joint residential houses of the parties. These circumstances, prima facie, lend assurance to the prosecution version regarding the identity of the appellant and diminish the likelihood of mistaken identification, particularly in view of the fact that the deceased, Said Haroon, and the co-accused, Said Ayub, were real brothers. However, the question of false implication, particularly with regard to the specific role of firing attributed to the appellant, must ultimately be determined in the light of the evidence available on record.

6. To substantiate the charge against the present appellant, the prosecution primarily relied upon the ocular account furnished by the complainant, Haroon-ur-Rashid (PW-10), Kalim Ullah (PW-11), another son of the deceased, and Umar Farooq (PW-12), son-in-law of the deceased. The prosecution further relied upon the dying declaration allegedly made by Said Haroon while he was alive and injured. In this regard, Dr. Badshahud-Din, who attended the injured at the hospital as a first responder, appeared as PW-4, whereas Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din Muhammad Naeem, ASI (PW-1), was examined to establish that the deceased, Said Haroon, while injured, lodged his report at Lal Qila Hospital in his presence, which forms the basis of the prosecution's reliance upon the same as a “dying declaration”. Besides the foregoing evidence, the prosecution also relied upon circumstantial evidence in the form of recoveries, including the alleged recovery of the weapon of offence, i.e., a .30-bore pistol, coupled with the corresponding Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL) report, which was relied upon to establish a match between the recovered pistol and the crime empties.

7. Haroon-ur-Rashid, son of the deceased, appeared before the learned trial Court as PW-10. In his deposition, he stated that, on the fateful night, at Maghrib time, he, along with other inmates of the house, was present at home when an altercation ensued between him and his uncle, co-accused Said Ayub, over a land dispute. In the meanwhile, his father, the deceased Said Haroon, intervened to pacify the parties. However, the appellant, Muhammad Salar, and his father, co-accused Said Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din Ayub, allegedly armed with pistols, opened indiscriminate fire upon the complainant-party, as a result of which his father sustained firearm injuries. A similar account was furnished by Kalim Ullah (PW-11), another son of the deceased, who also attributed the firing to both accused persons and deposed that their firing caused multiple injuries to his father on different parts of his body. It is, however, pertinent to observe that, in the initial report lodged by the deceased while injured, in the form of a Murasila, which formed the basis of the instant FIR, the specific role of firing upon the deceased was attributed to the present appellant, Muhammad Salar. Umar Farooq, son-in-law of the deceased, appeared before the learned trial Court as PW-12. In his examination-in-chief, he corroborated the accounts furnished by the other two eyewitnesses and specifically attributed the infliction of multiple firearm injuries upon Said Haroon to the present appellant, Muhammad Salar, which ultimately resulted in his death. All these witnesses were subjected to lengthy cross-examination; however, their credibility, particularly regarding the specific Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din role of firing attributed to the appellant, remained unimpaired.

8. Since the occurrence took place inside the joint residential houses of the parties at Maghrib time, the presence of the inmates, particularly the male members of the family, was quite natural and cannot be termed improbable. In this regard, guidance may be sought from the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Nadeem Ramzan v. State, wherein it was held that the presence of the deceased’s husband and brother-in-law, being residents and inmates of the house where the occurrence took place, rendered them natural witnesses. Their close relationship with the deceased and the accused also militated against the possibility of mistaken identity. The Court further observed that the consistent ocular account furnished by the eyewitnesses stood corroborated by the medical evidence regarding the time of occurrence, the weapon used and the location of the injuries. The principle enunciated therein lends support to the prosecution’s stance regarding the natural presence of the witnesses and the identification of the Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din appellant, subject to the overall assessment of the evidence available on record [ ]. A similar view was expressed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan in Muhammad Akbar alias Bola and others v. State and others, wherein the prosecution had produced three eyewitnesses, two of whom were natural witnesses being inmates of the house where the occurrence took place, while one of them had also sustained injuries during the incident. Their consistent ocular account was found to have received sufficient corroboration from the medical evidence. The principle laid down therein further supports the evidentiary worth of natural witnesses whose presence at the place of occurrence is established by the surrounding circumstances and whose testimony finds corroboration from the medical evidence [ ].

9. As regards the dying declaration of the deceased, Said Haroon, who was injured at the time of making the statement, the relevant provision was previously contained in section 32 of the Evidence Act, 1872, and is now embodied in Article 46 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984. Under the said “ Nadeem Ramzan v/s State” reported as 2018 SCMR 149 “ Muhammad Akbar alias Bola & others v/s State & others” reported as 2019 SCMR 2036. Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din provision, a statement made by a person who has died is relevant where it relates to the cause of his death or to any circumstance of the transaction that resulted in his death, particularly where the cause of death is a matter-in-issue. Although a dying declaration constitutes an exception to the general rule against hearsay, its evidentiary worth must be assessed with due care and caution. While superior Courts have consistently emphasized the need for strict scrutiny of such evidence, it is equally settled that a dying declaration, if found genuine, voluntary and trustworthy, may constitute substantive evidence and form the basis of conviction without independent corroboration. Its acceptability, however, depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case, including the condition of the declarant, the circumstances in which the statement was made and its inherent credibility. The principles governing the evidentiary value of a dying declaration and the circumstances in which a conviction may lawfully be founded upon it have been elaborated by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan in a number of judgments. Reference, in Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din this regard, may be made to Farman Ullah v. Qadeem Khan and another (2001 SCMR 1474), wherein the governing principles were discussed as follows:- (i) No specified forum is available before whom dying declaration is required to be made;
(ii) There is no bar that it cannot be made before a private person;
(iii) There is no legal requirement that the declaration must be read over or it must be signed by its maker;
(iv) It should be influence free;
(vi) In order to prove such declaration, the person by whom it was recorded should be examined;
(vii) Such declaration becomes substantive evidence when it is proved that it was made by the deceased;
(viii) Corroboration of dying declaration is not a rule of law, but requirement of prudence and such declaration when proved by cogent evidence can be made a base for conviction.

Likewise, in Muhammad Saeed and another v. State and another (2024 SCMR 1421), the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan, while discussing the evidentiary value and relevance of a dying declaration, emphasized that its probative worth must be assessed in the light of the peculiar facts and circumstances of each case, by observing as follows:- “That under Article 46 of the Qanun-e- Shahadat Order, 1984, the sanctity of a Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din dying declaration has to be evaluated with great care and caution and the evidence consisting of dying declaration has to be appreciated with due diligence. dying declaration is a question of fact which has to be determined on the facts of each case. To find out truth or falsity of a dying declaration, a case is generally to be considered in all its physical environment and circumstances. A dying declaration can be made before a private person but it should be free from any influence and the person before whom it is made has to be examined. It is necessary to ascertain that the dying declaration was made honestly, its maker was in a fit state of mind to make the statement, its maker was free from outside influence, its maker was fearing death and had made truthful statement.”

In support of the same rational, further reliance can also made to case law titled “Muhammad Abdullah v/s Muhammad Sapdar Khan & another” reported as 1973 SCMR 26 and case titled “Muhammad Ashraf Khan Tareen & another v/s State & another” reported as 1996 SCMR 1747.

10. In the case in hand, the deceased, Said Haroon, while injured, was brought to Lal Qila Hospital by Haroon-ur-Rashid (PW-10), his son and an eyewitness to the occurrence, in a seriously injured condition. He was initially examined by Dr. Badshah-ud-Din (PW-4), who was subsequently reexamined as RPW-4. The post-mortem report, duly Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din verified by the said doctor, attributed the death to a firearm injury on the left side of the chest, which had lacerated the lower lobe of the lung, causing clotted hemothorax and empyema, ultimately leading to cardiopulmonary arrest and death. During crossexamination, PW-4 acknowledged the presence of police officials at the hospital and confirmed that, at the relevant time, the injured was conscious and well-oriented in time and space. The record further reveals that the initial report of the deceased, relied upon by the prosecution as his dying declaration, bore the thumb impression of the declarant, duly verified by his son, Haroon-ur-Rashid. Muhammad Naeem Khan, ASI (PW-1), who recorded the statement, also signed the report as its scribe. Significantly, PW-1 deposed that, before recording the statement of the injured, he had sought the opinion of the attending doctor regarding his fitness to make a statement through an application (Ex. PW- 1/1). These circumstances are relevant to determining whether the deceased was in a fit state of mind to make the statement and whether the declaration was recorded in a reliable manner. In Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din view of the above-referred overwhelming evidence of prosecution, dying declaration in the present case cannot be discarded by any stretch of imagination qua guilt of the present appellant/accused and presence of the firearm injury on the person of the deceased then injured. Reliance may further be placed upon the judgment of this Court in Mashad Ali v. State, wherein the dying declaration was found reliable, inter-alia, because it bore the thumb impression of the deceased and the signature of its author. The Medical Officer’s testimony also supported the deceased’s consciousness and orientation at the time of making the statement, while the defence, despite cross-examining both the doctor and the author of the Murasila, failed to elicit anything suggesting that the deceased was incapable of making a statement. The Court further took into account that the injured had survived for more than fifteen days after the occurrence, which supported the conclusion that he remained conscious, oriented in time and space, and capable of making a statement. The principle laid down therein lends support to the evidentiary value of a Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din dying declaration where its execution, the declarant’s fitness and the circumstances in which it was recorded stand established through reliable evidence.[ ].

11. Learned counsel for appellant was also critical of the fact that all the three eyewitnesses of ocular-account were closely related to the deceased, being her real sons and son-in-law. However, mere relationship between witnesses and the deceased would not be sufficient to damage their evidence altogether. Reliance may further be placed upon the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Aqil v. State, wherein it was held that a witness may be termed an interested witness only where he or she stands to gain some benefit from the conviction of the accused. A natural witness, whose presence at the place of occurrence is probable in the circumstances of the case, cannot be branded as an interested witness merely on account of relationship or being the only available eyewitness [ ].The Hon’ble apex Court in the case of “Abdur Rauf Vs. State & another” has held that “relationship by itself is no ground to discard or discredit testimony “Mashad Ali v/s State & another” reported as 2021 P Cr. LJ Note 16. “Aqil v/s State” reported as 2023 SCMR 831. Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din of an eye-witnesses unless he is shown to be partisan and interested witness” [ ]. It is an intrinsic value of a statement of a prosecution witness which is to be taken into account and not his/her relationship. It is not a rule of thumb that an interested or related witness will always tell lie and independent witness truth, rather testimony of a witness in each case is required to be adjudged in light of its own facts and circumstances. If it is established on record that a witness had a motive to implicate an accused person falsely in criminal a case, then in such eventuality independent corroboration may be sought from other evidence. In the present case, there is nothing on record to suggest any previous blood feud or other bitterness of serious nature between the parties, except the one referred to above i.e. land dispute, hence, these eye-witnesses had no motive for false implication of the present appellant. Likewise, same rational of law was earlier expounded by the Hon’ble apex Court in Amal Sherin’s case by holding that “mere relationship of a witness with deceased would not discredit his/her testimony” [ ]. Refence can also be made to case titled “Khalid v/s State” [ ].

“Abdur Rauf Vs. State and another” reported as 2003 SCMR 522. “Amal Sherin & another v/s State” reported as PLD 2004 Supreme Court 371. “Khalid v/s State” reported as 2024 SCMR 1474. Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din In light of ratio-decidendi expounded in the aforesaid judgments of various Courts, the ocular-account furnished by PW-10, PW-11 and PW-12, respectively, cannot be discarded on the sole ground of their close relationship with the deceased, when otherwise they appear to be truthful witnesses.

12. The medical evidence pertaining to the deceased, who was initially injured, is consistent with the prosecution version regarding the receipt of a firearm injury. It lends corroboration to the ocular account furnished by PW-10, PW-11 and PW-12 regarding the nature of the injury and the alleged use of weapon of offence. The learned trial Court, therefore, rightly considered the medical evidence alongside the ocular account while assessing the prosecution case against the appellant. Even otherwise, it is settled proposition of law that “medical evidence may confirm direct or ocular account and by all means it is corroboratory in nature” [ ].

13. As regards the circumstantial evidence, suffice it to observe that the appellant was arrested in Abdul Rashid v/s The State” reported as 2019 P Cr. LJ 1456 Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din the instant case on 15.09.2021, and on the same day, a .30-bore pistol was allegedly recovered at his pointation vide recovery memo (Ex. PW-5/4). Earlier, during the investigation, two crime empties had been secured from the place of occurrence. The FSL report (Ex. PW-7/27) confirms that the two 30 bore crime empties duly marked as C-1 and C-2, were fired from 30 bore pistol No. Nill marked as “A” in question. The delay in dispatching the crime empties to the FSL, by itself, is not necessarily fatal to the prosecution case, particularly where the accused was subsequently arrested and the remaining evidence is found reliable. However, the evidentiary significance of the recovery and forensic report must be assessed in conjunction with the ocular account and the other circumstances established on record.

14. The motive for the occurrence was alleged to be a dispute over landed property. In support thereof, the prosecution relied upon the statements of the complainant, now deceased, and the eyewitnesses examined as PW-10, PW-11 and PW-12, respectively. Despite lengthy and searching cross-examination by the defence, their testimony Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din regarding the alleged motive remained unimpeached. In case titled “State v/s Muhammad Sharif”, the Hon’ble apex Court has held that the “motive is a double-edged weapon which cuts both sides in alike manner” [ ].

15. Upon an overall assessment of the prosecution evidence, this Court is persuaded that the appellant’s guilt has been established. However, the question of sentence calls for separate consideration. An admitted feature of the case is that the occurrence stemmed from a heated altercation between the deceased’s son and the co-accused, Said Ayub, who is the appellant’s father, over a land dispute. The circumstances suggest that the incident occurred at the spur of the moment, without prior planning or premeditation on the appellant’s part. These aspects warrant careful consideration in determining whether the sentence of imprisonment for life awarded to the appellant calls for any interference. Reference can be made to the judgment of Hon’ble apex Court rendered in case titled “Zeeshan alias Shani V/S State” reported as PLD “State VS. Muhammad Sharif and others” reported as 1995 SCMR 635. Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din 2017 S.C 165, wherein it was held that “in eventuality, when an accused person committed an offence without any premeditation or planning and in the heat of domestic issue caused a death of deceased. In such circumstances, his/her case would come within clause (c) of section 302 PPC. Conviction of accused recorded U/S 302 (b) PPC was altered to one U/S 302 (c) PPC and consequently, his sentence of life imprisonment was reduced to ten years imprisonment. It is pertinent to observe that the prosecution case itself suggests that the occurrence took place at the spur of the moment during an altercation arising out of a land dispute, without any apparent premeditation or prior planning on the part of the appellant. The record further indicates that the deceased sustained a single firearm injury on a vital part of his body. Although this circumstance, by itself, does not conclusively negate an intention to kill, it may be considered alongside the suddenness of the occurrence and the surrounding circumstances while determining the appropriate sentence. It is also evident from the record that there was some variation between the Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din initial report of the deceased, who was then injured, and the testimonies of his two sons, examined as PW-10 and PW-11. In his initial report, the deceased specifically attributed the firearm injury on a vital part of his body to the present appellant, Muhammad Salar. However, the said eyewitnesses deposed that both the accused, namely Said Ayub, their uncle, and the present appellant, resorted to indiscriminate firing at the complainant-party, resulting in firearm injuries to their father. This variance, in itself, does not materially undermine the prosecution case regarding the appellant’s role in causing the fatal injury. Nevertheless, it constitutes a relevant circumstance to be considered, along with the other mitigating factors, while determining the appropriate sentence. In view of the foregoing mitigating circumstances, this Court finds the case to warrant reduction of the appellant’s sentence from imprisonment for life to twelve years’ rigorous imprisonment U/S 302(c), P.P.C.

16. Thus, the minor discrepancies and lacunae in the prosecution evidence, as discussed hereinabove, do not suffice to warrant the outright Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din acquittal of the appellant. However, these aspects may be taken into consideration while determining the appropriate sentence, as observed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Mst. Bevi v. Ghulam Shabbir and another (1980 SCMR 859), wherein it was held as follows:- “It has been held in some cases that the principle underlying the concept of benefit of doubt can in addition to the consideration of question of guilt or otherwise, be pressed also in matter of sentence. As a definite motive was asserted against the respondent and the same has failed, keeping in view all the circumstances of this case, it would not be necessary to impose the capita' punishment. Therefore, while finding him guilty; under section 302, P. P. C. he is sentenced to transportation for life should be awarded as compensation.”

A similar principle was enunciated by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Mir Muhammad alias Miro v. State (2009 SCMR 1188). Reliance may also be placed on Muhammad Ayaz Khan v. Murtaza and others (2008 SCMR 984) and Kamran Ullah v. State and another (2020 SCMR 1214), wherein the Hon’ble apex Court further elucidated the relevant principles governing the appreciation of evidentiary deficiencies and their bearing on the question of sentence.

Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din 17. In view of the above discussion and exposition of law, the instant criminal appeal is partially allowed, the impugned judgment dated 21.12.2024 of the Court of learned Additional Sessions Judge, Samarbagh, Camp Court at Lal Qila, Dir Lower, rendered in case FIR No. 165 dated 12.8.2021, U/Ss 302, 34 PPC registered at Police Station Lal Qila, District Dir Lower, is modified to the extent by converting the sentence of life imprisonment awarded to appellant/convict namely Muhammad Salar son of Said Ayub U/S 302 (b) PPC as Ta’zir to twelve (12) years rigorous imprisonment U/S 302 (c) PPC. Rest of impugned order/judgment of learned trial Court to the extent of imposition of compensation, along with benefit of section 382-B Cr.P.C shall remain intact.

18. As regards the connected Criminal Appeal No. 395-M of 2024, arising out of the separate trial in Sessions Case No. 16/AA of 2021, emanating from FIR No. 208 dated 15.09.2021, registered U/S 15 of the Arms Act at Police Station Lal Qila, Dir Lower, the learned trial Court, vide separate judgment dated 21.12.2024, directed that the sentence awarded Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din therein shall run concurrently with the sentence of imprisonment for life imposed in the main murder case arising out of FIR No. 165. In view of the reduction of the appellant’s sentence in the main case to twelve years’ rigorous imprisonment U/S 302(c), P.P.C., the sentence in the connected case shall also run concurrently. Consequently, upon completion of the said period of imprisonment, the appellant shall be dealt with in accordance with law in the connected case. The connected Criminal Appeal No. 395-M of 2024 is, accordingly, disposed of in the above terms.

19. Insofar as the connected Criminal Appeal bearing No. 18-M of 2025, directed against the acquittal of accused/respondent Said Ayub is concerned. Bare perusal of the initial report lodged by the complainant, now deceased, reveals that no overt act was attributed to the accused/respondent, except his mere presence at the joint residential house where the occurrence took place. In the absence of reliable evidence establishing his participation in the commission of the offence, the learned trial Court was justified in extending the benefit of doubt to him. It is a settled principle of criminal jurisprudence that an Nawab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din acquittal further reinforces the presumption of innocence, and an appellate Court would be slow to interfere unless the findings recorded by the trial Court are arbitrary, capricious, perverse, or contrary to the evidence on record. No such infirmity has been demonstrated in the impugned judgment.
Consequently, the connected Criminal Appeal No. 18-M of 2025, being devoid of merit, is dismissed.

20. In view of the partial acceptance of the criminal appeal preferred by the appellant/convict, Muhammad Salar, the connected Criminal Revision No. 06-M of 2025, filed by the complainant/ petitioner seeking enhancement of his sentence, has become infructuous. Consequently, the said criminal revision petition is also dismissed.
21. These are reasons for our short order of even date.
